questions.question_text:
Find $\mathrm{Var}(X)$ for the distribution below.
$\begin{array}{c|cccc} x & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.4 & 0.3 & 0.2 & 0.1 \end{array}$

options.why: Gave $E(X^{2})$ and did not subtract $\mu^{2}$.
Gave $\mu^{2}$ instead of the difference $E(X^{2})-\mu^{2}$.
Gave the mean $\mu$ rather than the variance.

questions.question_text:
Find $\sigma$ for the distribution below, correct to two decimal places.
$\begin{array}{c|ccc} x & 1 & 4 & 9 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.5 & 0.3 & 0.2 \end{array}$

options.why: Stopped at the variance and did not take the square root.
Took the square root of $E(X^{2})$ without subtracting $\mu^{2}$ first.
Took the square root of the mean instead of the square root of the variance.

questions.question_text:
The random variable $X$ has mean $\mu=4.2$.
Find $\mathrm{Var}(X)$.
$\begin{array}{c|cccc} x & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.25 & 0.4 & 0.25 & 0.1 \end{array}$

options.why: Gave $E(X^{2})$ without subtracting $\mu^{2}$.
Gave $\mu^{2}$, the quantity that should have been subtracted.
Went one step too far and gave the standard deviation.

questions.question_text:
Use $\mathrm{Var}(X)=\sum (x-\mu)^{2}P(x)$ to find the variance.
$\begin{array}{c|ccc} x & 1 & 3 & 5 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.3 & 0.5 & 0.2 \end{array}$

options.why: Gave the standard deviation instead of the variance.
Forgot to square the deviations, and $\sum (x-\mu)P(x)$ is always $0$.
Computed $E(X^{2})$ and never subtracted $\mu^{2}$.

questions.question_text:
The random variables $A$ and $B$ below both have mean $2$.
Which has the greater standard deviation?
$A: \begin{array}{c|ccc} a & 0 & 2 & 4 \\ \hline P(A=a) & 0.25 & 0.5 & 0.25 \end{array}$
$B: \begin{array}{c|ccc} b & 0 & 2 & 4 \\ \hline P(B=b) & 0.4 & 0.2 & 0.4 \end{array}$

options.text: $B$, because more of its probability sits at $0$ and $4$, giving $\mathrm{Var}(B)=3.2$ against $\mathrm{Var}(A)=2$.
$A$, because its middle value carries the highest probability.
options.why: Judged spread by the height of the peak rather than by the variance.

options.text: Neither, because both distributions have mean $2$.
options.why: Assumed equal means force equal spread.

options.text: $A$, because $A$ has the larger value of $E(X^{2})$.
options.why: Compared $E(X^{2})$, and in any case $A$'s value of $6$ is the smaller of the two.

questions.solution_text:
$E(A^{2})=0(0.25)+4(0.5)+16(0.25)$
$=6$
$\mathrm{Var}(A)=6-2^{2}$
$=2$
$E(B^{2})=0(0.4)+4(0.2)+16(0.4)$
$=7.2$
$\mathrm{Var}(B)=7.2-2^{2}$
$=3.2$
$B$ has the greater variance and so the greater standard deviation.

Given that $E(X)>0$, find $E(X)$.

questions.question_text:
Find $\sigma$ for the distribution below, correct to two decimal places.
$\begin{array}{c|cccc} x & -3 & -1 & 2 & 4 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.2 & 0.3 & 0.4 & 0.1 \end{array}$

options.why: Stopped at the variance and did not take the square root.
Took $\sqrt{E(X^{2})}$, forgetting to subtract $\mu^{2}=0.09$ first.
Took the square root of the mean $0.3$ instead of the square root of the variance.

questions.question_text:
The probability distribution is believed to be modelled by
$\begin{array}{c|cccc}r&1&2&3&4\\\hline P(X=r)&\dfrac{1}{3}&\dfrac{1}{6}&\dfrac{1}{12}&\dfrac{5}{12}\end{array}$
What is the variance?

options.why: Uses the second moment alone and does not subtract the square of the expectation.
Rounds or estimates the result without matching the exact variance from the table.
Subtracts an incorrect squared mean from the second moment.
